contents.html: The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. contents.html: The document highlights examples for implementing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) in a manner that complements the use of other NIST security and privacy risk management standards, guidelines, and practices. These examples include support for an Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) approach in alignment with OMB and FISMA requirements that agency heads “manage risk commensurate with the magnitude of harm that would result from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of a federal information system or federal information.” The use of the Cybersecurity Framework’s components enable discussion about the various types of risk that might occur within federal organizations and promote conversations about how to determine the likelihood and potential consequences of risk events. These activities can then be combined with those described in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-37, Revision 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations; SP 800-39, Managing Information Security Risk; and other guidelines to form a comprehensive risk-based approach for security and privacy.
contents.html_ja: 本文書は、Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity（サイバーセキュリティフレームワークとして知られる）を、NIST の他のセキュリティおよびプライバシーのリスクマネジメントに関する標準、ガイドライン、プラクティスを補完する形で実装するための例を取り上げます。これらの例には、エンタープライズリスクマネジメント（ERM）のアプローチへの支援が含まれ、これは「連邦情報システムまたは連邦情報への、不正なアクセス、使用、開示、中断、変更、破壊によって生じる損害の大きさに見合ったリスクを管理する」ことを機関の長に求める OMB および FISMA の要件に沿ったものです。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークの構成要素を用いることで、連邦組織内で生じうるさまざまな種類のリスクについて議論でき、リスク事象の可能性と起こりうる結果をどのように判断するかについての対話が促されます。これらの活動は、NIST Special Publication（SP）800-37 Revision 2『Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations』、SP 800-39『Managing Information Security Risk』およびその他のガイドラインに記述された活動と組み合わせることで、セキュリティとプライバシーに対する包括的なリスクベースのアプローチを形成できます。

contents.html: This risk-based approach will assist agencies in determining the risks that are relevant to its mission throughout the operational lifecycle and apply an appropriate type and degree of resources to treat those risks to an acceptable level. Examples in this publication will demonstrate the use of the Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF), and other models to evaluate and report agency goals and progress and to inform tailoring activities for managing cybersecurity risk appropriately. Use of a comprehensive cybersecurity risk-based approach, as demonstrated through these examples, supports agencies’ activities to meet their concurrent obligations to comply with the requirements of FISMA and Executive Order (EO) 13800.
contents.html_ja: このリスクベースのアプローチは、機関が、運用ライフサイクル全体を通じて自らの任務に関連するリスクを特定し、それらのリスクを許容可能な水準まで対処するために適切な種類と程度のリソースを充てる助けとなります。本刊行物の例は、サイバーセキュリティフレームワーク、NIST Risk Management Framework（RMF）、およびその他のモデルを用いて、機関の目標と進捗を評価・報告し、サイバーセキュリティリスクを適切に管理するためのテーラリング活動に情報を提供する方法を示します。これらの例で示されるような、包括的でリスクベースのサイバーセキュリティアプローチを用いることは、機関が FISMA および大統領令（EO）13800 の要件に準拠するという、並行する義務を果たすための活動を支えます。

contents.html: All federal agencies are entrusted with safeguarding the information contained in their systems and ensuring that those systems operate securely and reliably. It is vital that agency personnel at all levels manage their assets wisely and address cybersecurity risks effectively. To do that, agencies need a holistic approach to their enterprises’ risk management that includes timely, streamlined approaches and automated tools.

contents.html: As part of its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act as amended (FISMA), the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) develops standards and guidelines—including minimum requirements—to provide adequate information security for federal information and information systems [1]. This suite of security and privacy risk management standards and guidelines provides guidance for an integrated, organization-wide program to manage information security risk.
contents.html_ja: National Institute of Standards and Technology（NIST）は、改正された Federal Information Security Management Act（FISMA）に基づく法令上の責務の一環として、連邦情報および連邦情報システムに適切な情報セキュリティを提供するための標準とガイドライン（最低限の要件を含む）を策定しています [1]。この一連のセキュリティおよびプライバシーのリスクマネジメントに関する標準とガイドラインは、情報セキュリティリスクを管理するための、組織全体にわたる統合的なプログラムに向けた指針を提供します。

contents.html: NIST produced this report to assist federal agencies in strengthening their cybersecurity risk management processes by highlighting example approaches for implementing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) [5]. Developed by NIST in close collaboration with private and public sectors, the Cybersecurity Framework is a risk-based approach used voluntarily by organizations across the United States. Initially developed to address cybersecurity challenges in the Nation’s Critical Infrastructure (CI) sectors, the voluntary Framework is used by a variety of organizations across the world. The Cybersecurity Framework aligns with and complements NIST’s suite of security and privacy risk management standards and guidelines.
contents.html_ja: NIST は、Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity（サイバーセキュリティフレームワークとして知られる）を実装するためのアプローチ例を示すことで、連邦機関がサイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメントのプロセスを強化できるよう支援するために、本報告書を作成しました [5]。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークは、NIST が民間部門および公共部門と緊密に協力して策定したもので、米国全土の組織が自主的に用いているリスクベースのアプローチです。当初は国の重要インフラストラクチャ（CI）分野におけるサイバーセキュリティ上の課題に対処するために策定されましたが、この自主的なフレームワークは、世界中のさまざまな組織で使われています。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークは、NIST の一連のセキュリティおよびプライバシーのリスクマネジメントに関する標準とガイドラインと整合し、それらを補完します。

contents.html: As part of its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act as amended (FISMA), NIST develops standards and guidelines—including minimum requirements—to support information security for agency operations and assets. NIST guidelines fulfill the requirements of FISMA and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-130, and are used by agencies to develop, implement, and maintain cybersecurity and privacy programs [6]. They include Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS), Special Publications (SPs), and NIST Interagency Reports (NISTIRs).
contents.html_ja: NIST は、改正された Federal Information Security Management Act（FISMA）に基づく法令上の責務の一環として、機関の業務と資産の情報セキュリティを支援するための標準とガイドライン（最低限の要件を含む）を策定しています。NIST のガイドラインは FISMA および Office of Management and Budget（OMB）Circular A-130 の要件を満たすもので、機関がサイバーセキュリティおよびプライバシーのプログラムを策定、実装、維持するために用いられています [6]。これらには、Federal Information Processing Standards（FIPS）、Special Publications（SP）、NIST Interagency Reports（NISTIR）が含まれます。

contents.html: The Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014 formally updated NIST’s role to include identifying and developing cybersecurity risk frameworks for voluntary use by critical infrastructure (CI) owners and operators. The frameworks’ subsequent widespread use and adoption demonstrates their universal applicability [7]. That statute’s assignments included work that NIST began in February 2013 as a result of Executive Order (EO) 13636, Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity [8], which directed the Department of Commerce to lead the development of a voluntary framework to reduce CI cybersecurity risks. Accordingly, NIST convened industry, academia, and government sectors to develop the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) that consists of standards, methodologies, procedures, and processes that align policy, business, and technological approaches to address cybersecurity risks [5]. It offers a high-level vocabulary for cybersecurity risk management along with a set of cybersecurity outcomes and a methodology to assess and manage those outcomes.
contents.html_ja: Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014 は、重要インフラストラクチャ（CI）の所有者および運用者が自主的に利用するサイバーセキュリティリスクのフレームワークを特定し策定することを、NIST の役割に正式に加えました。これらのフレームワークがその後広く利用され採用されていることは、その普遍的な適用可能性を示しています [7]。この法律が定めた任務には、大統領令（EO）13636『Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity』[8] の結果として NIST が 2013年2月に開始した作業が含まれていました。この大統領令は、CI のサイバーセキュリティリスクを低減するための自主的なフレームワークの策定を商務省が主導するよう指示したものです。これを受けて NIST は、産業界、学術界、政府の各部門を招集し、サイバーセキュリティリスクに対処するために政策、事業、技術のアプローチを整合させる標準、方法論、手順、プロセスからなる Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity（サイバーセキュリティフレームワークとして知られる）を策定しました [5]。このフレームワークは、サイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメントのための高水準の語彙とともに、一連のサイバーセキュリティの成果と、それらの成果を評価し管理するための方法論を提供します。

contents.html: The increasing frequency, creativity, and variety of cybersecurity attacks means that all organizations should place great emphasis on managing cybersecurity risk as a part of their Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) programs to fulfill their mission and business objectives. By integrating the Cybersecurity Framework with NIST cybersecurity risk management standards and guidelines already in wide use at various organizational levels, agencies can develop, implement, and continuously improve agency-wide cybersecurity risk management processes that inform strategic, operational, and other enterprise risk decisions.<sup>1</sup>
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティ攻撃の頻度の増加、手口の巧妙化、種類の多様化により、すべての組織は、自らの任務と事業目標を果たすために、エンタープライズリスクマネジメント（ERM）プログラムの一部としてサイバーセキュリティリスクの管理を重視すべきです。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークを、組織のさまざまな階層ですでに広く使われている NIST のサイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメントの標準およびガイドラインと統合することで、機関は、戦略上、運用上、その他のエンタープライズのリスクに関する意思決定に情報を提供する、機関全体のサイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメントプロセスを策定、実装し、継続的に改善できます。<sup>1</sup>

contents.html: Organizations manage many types of risk. They develop policies to identify, assess, and mitigate adverse effects with cybersecurity dependencies across various types of enterprise risks. In addition to cybersecurity risks, other typical enterprise risks include safety, financial, program, acquisitions, supply chain, and privacy. Many of these other types of risk may also have cybersecurity risk implications or be impacted by cybersecurity. Some employ different terminologies and risk management approaches to make decisions. OMB Circular A-123 establishes an expectation for federal agencies to proactively consider and address risks through an integrated, organization-level view of events, conditions, or scenarios that impact mission achievement. Organizations may have established a unique lexicon for ERM that should be considered when communicating risks at the organization level. This necessitates coordination with existing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) functions on how to best incorporate and communicate cybersecurity risks at the organization and system levels.
contents.html_ja: 組織は多くの種類のリスクを管理しています。組織は、さまざまな種類のエンタープライズリスクにまたがってサイバーセキュリティへの依存関係を持つ悪影響を特定、評価、軽減するためのポリシーを策定します。サイバーセキュリティリスクのほかにも、典型的なエンタープライズリスクには、安全、財務、プログラム、調達、サプライチェーン、プライバシーがあります。これらの他の種類のリスクの多くは、サイバーセキュリティリスクにも関係しうるものであり、サイバーセキュリティの影響を受ける場合もあります。意思決定に際して、異なる用語やリスクマネジメントのアプローチを用いる組織もあります。OMB Circular A-123 は、任務の達成に影響を与える事象、状況、シナリオを組織レベルで統合的に捉えることで、連邦機関がリスクに先回りして対処することへの期待を定めています。組織は ERM について独自の用語体系を確立している場合があり、組織レベルでリスクを伝える際にはそれを考慮すべきです。このため、サイバーセキュリティリスクを組織レベルとシステムレベルでどのように取り込み、伝えるのが最善かについて、既存のエンタープライズリスクマネジメント（ERM）部門と調整する必要があります。

contents.html: The Cybersecurity Framework Core’s five “Functions”—Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover—offer a way to organize cybersecurity risk management activities at their highest levels that can be applied across risk management disciplines. These same five words are further classified into more specific meanings with the Cybersecurity Framework Core, enabling precise and efficient implementation of any enterprise risk decisions impacting cybersecurity. Many stakeholders from various parts of an organization can understand and may already use these five words in the context of risk decisions. Different disciplines communicate risk at differing levels of breadth and depth, so the Cybersecurity Framework outcomes help facilitate discussions.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのコアにある 5 つの「機能」（Identify、Protect、Detect、Respond、Recover）は、リスクマネジメントの各分野に適用できる、最上位の水準でサイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメント活動を整理する方法を提供します。これら同じ 5 つの語は、サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのコアの中でさらに具体的な意味へと分類されており、サイバーセキュリティに影響するあらゆるエンタープライズのリスクに関する意思決定を、正確かつ効率的に実装できるようにします。組織のさまざまな部署の多くの関係者は、リスクに関する意思決定の文脈でこれら 5 つの語を理解でき、すでに使っている場合もあります。分野によってリスクを伝える際の幅と深さは異なるため、サイバーセキュリティフレームワークの成果は議論を円滑にする助けとなります。

contents.html: While Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) and other cybersecurity professionals in federal agencies are encouraged to use these five functions as a way to engage, organize, and explain cybersecurity approaches to the agency’s external stakeholders, executive leadership, and employees and to integrate cybersecurity concepts into other organizational areas, traditional risk management language and concepts should likewise be communicated to the more technical ranks of the organization. The five Functions offer an organizing principle for CISOs to gather risk tolerance<sup>3</sup> perspectives from system owners and functional leads while preparing to engage strategies to address risk considerations at a higher level in the organization.

contents.html: Agencies can align and merge internal and external requirements using the structure of the Core. For instance, a federal agency may need to abide by FISMA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Security Rule, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, and their own cybersecurity policy. Applicable excerpts of these laws, guidelines, policies, and objectives can be aligned with the various Functions, Categories, and Subcategories of the Core. That can help agencies to determine where requirements overlap and/or conflict so that they can consider alternative approaches—including modifying cybersecurity requirements within that agency’s control.

contents.html: Implementation Tiers are not prescriptive, and there is no set requirement for an organization and all its sub-organizations to operate at Implementation Tier 4. Rather, Implementation Tiers can be used for informed trade-off analysis since there is a corresponding cost and risk tolerance associated with each Implementation Tier. For example, to balance finite resources across all agency cybersecurity considerations, it may be appropriate to operate at Implementation Tier 2 in one part of an agency so that the agency can afford to operate at Implementation Tier 4 elsewhere. One way that federal agencies may apply these trade-offs is via FIPS-199 categorizations [12]. An agency might view FIPS-199 High Impact and High Value Asset<sup>8</sup> (HVA) systems as appropriate for higher Implementation Tiers. Conversely, the agency may determine that operating at a lower Implementation Tier for FIPS-199 Low Impact categorized systems is acceptable.
contents.html_ja: 実装ティアは規範的なものではなく、組織とそのすべての下位組織が実装ティア 4 で運用するという決まった要件はありません。むしろ、各実装ティアにはそれに応じたコストとリスク許容度が伴うため、実装ティアは、情報に基づくトレードオフ分析に用いることができます。たとえば、機関のすべてのサイバーセキュリティ上の考慮事項にわたって限られたリソースのバランスを取るために、機関のある部分を実装ティア 2 で運用することで、ほかの部分を実装ティア 4 で運用する余裕を確保することが適切な場合があります。連邦機関がこうしたトレードオフを適用する方法の一つは、FIPS-199 のカテゴリ分類によるものです [12]。機関は、FIPS-199 の High Impact のシステムや高価値資産<sup>8</sup>（HVA）のシステムに、より高い実装ティアが適切であると考えることがあります。逆に、FIPS-199 の Low Impact に分類されるシステムについては、より低い実装ティアでの運用が許容できると機関が判断する場合もあります。

contents.html: The Core taxonomy of cybersecurity outcomes that are captured in Subcategories provides a logical structure to organize cybersecurity operations within an agency—specifically, how work is assigned, tracked, and measured and how personnel empowerment and accountability is managed.

contents.html: The Cybersecurity Framework provides a way to assign cybersecurity responsibilities to units or individuals in an organization, including external entities with risk management roles. That allows executives to specify tasks, responsibilities, and risk management strategies. It also enables executives to empower units and individuals and to reward them appropriately. If parts of cybersecurity operations are not performing as intended, or if risk is above set threshold levels, the Cybersecurity Framework structure helps managers trace and investigate the situation and hold relevant units and individuals accountable.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークは、リスクマネジメントの役割を持つ外部の主体を含め、組織内の部署や個人にサイバーセキュリティの責任を割り当てる方法を提供します。これにより、経営幹部は、タスク、責任、リスクマネジメント戦略を明示できます。また、部署や個人に権限を与え、適切に報いることもできます。サイバーセキュリティ運用の一部が意図したとおりに機能していない場合や、リスクが設定された閾値を上回っている場合には、サイバーセキュリティフレームワークの構造が、管理者が状況を追跡して調査し、関係する部署や個人に説明責任を負わせる助けとなります。

contents.html: Using a Cybersecurity Framework Profile also may help identify opportunities for improving management of the organization’s cybersecurity workforce and how it achieves defined risk tolerance outcomes. One way to do that is by applying the NICE Workforce Framework from the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE), documented in SP 800-181 [13]. That workforce framework serves as a fundamental reference. It offers organizations a consistent lexicon for categorizing and describing cybersecurity work by category, specialty area, and work role, as well as a superset of cybersecurity knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs) and tasks for each work role. These elements support consistent organizational and sector communication for cybersecurity education, training, and workforce development. While the Cybersecurity Framework and the NICE Framework were developed separately, they complement each other by describing a hierarchical approach to achieving cybersecurity goals. The NICE program is in the process of determining alignment among Cybersecurity Framework subcategory outcomes and NICE Work Roles. As this work progresses, the alignment will help agencies document current and desired outcomes (based on Framework Core Subcategories) as well as the types of personnel that might have a role in accomplishing those outcomes. Furthermore, with the knowledge of the potential NICE work roles associated with a given set of outcomes, agencies will also be able to consider the NICE Framework’s definition of tasks associated with those roles and the relevant knowledge, skills, and abilities. This may help agencies to better define personnel requirements, qualifications, and evaluation criteria.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのプロファイルを用いることは、組織のサイバーセキュリティ人材の管理と、定義されたリスク許容度の成果をどのように達成するかを改善する機会を特定するのにも役立つ場合があります。その方法の一つは、SP 800-181 [13] に記載された National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education（NICE）の NICE Workforce Framework を適用することです。この人材フレームワークは、基本的な参照先として機能します。これは、サイバーセキュリティの業務をカテゴリ、専門分野、職務で分類して記述するための一貫した用語体系と、各職務のサイバーセキュリティの知識・技能・能力（KSA）およびタスクの上位集合を、組織に提供します。これらの要素は、サイバーセキュリティの教育、トレーニング、人材育成に関する、組織間および分野間の一貫したコミュニケーションを支えます。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークと NICE フレームワークは別々に策定されましたが、サイバーセキュリティの目標を達成するための階層的なアプローチを記述することで、互いを補完しています。NICE プログラムは、サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのサブカテゴリの成果と NICE の職務との整合を判断している段階にあります。この作業が進めば、その整合は、機関が現在の成果と望ましい成果（フレームワークのコアのサブカテゴリに基づく）、およびそれらの成果の達成に役割を持ちうる人員の種類を文書化するのに役立ちます。さらに、ある一連の成果に関連する NICE の職務の候補が分かれば、機関は、それらの職務に関連するタスクと、関連する知識・技能・能力に関する NICE フレームワークの定義も検討できるようになります。これは、機関が人員の要件、資格、評価基準をより適切に定義する助けとなる場合があります。

contents.html: In addition to determining the applicable work roles for a set of outcomes and associated security controls, the Cybersecurity Framework provides a manageable way to apportion responsibility for cybersecurity. Since the subcategory outcomes have already been mapped to the security controls in SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations, the responsibility for implementing and maintaining corresponding controls can also be assigned to these roles [14].

contents.html: When analyzing the desired cybersecurity outcomes associated with the Core’s Categories and Subcategories, some outcomes may be managed centrally and more cost-effectively for the entire agency rather than separately by each organizational unit. For example, an agency may determine that it is most beneficial and cost-effective for the entire agency to make Subcategory PR.AC-2 (i.e., “physical access to assets is managed and protected”) the responsibility of the Physical Security unit. These determinations can assist federal agencies in identifying candidates for common and hybrid controls as specified in SP 800-53.

contents.html: Another way for federal agencies to identify common cybersecurity controls is by identifying common assets and business processes. Managers of business units within agencies have key roles in identifying high-value assets and business processes. The ensuing discussions among business unit managers, the CISO, and other stakeholders regarding how to prioritize and protect these assets will likely recognize business units with similar assets or business processes that can utilize shared services. This can lead to the subsequent identification of common controls to secure assets and business processes across business units and potentially yield cost savings.
contents.html_ja: 連邦機関が共通のサイバーセキュリティ管理策を特定するもう一つの方法は、共通の資産と業務プロセスを特定することです。機関内の事業部門の管理者は、高価値資産と業務プロセスを特定するうえで重要な役割を担います。これらの資産とプロセスの優先順位付けと保護の方法について、事業部門の管理者、CISO、その他の関係者が議論を重ねることで、類似の資産や業務プロセスを持ち、共有サービスを利用できる事業部門が見つかる可能性が高くなります。これは、事業部門をまたいで資産と業務プロセスを保護するための共通管理策のその後の特定につながり、コスト削減をもたらす可能性があります。

contents.html: By aggregating cybersecurity findings, gaps, and vulnerabilities into a centralized record, agencies gain a combined view of cybersecurity risk and can make better informed risk decisions. Examples include determining how a system authorization decision might affect the agency as a whole, or how broader risk decisions might play out in a complex and connected infrastructure. An organization-wide record of risk enables consistent reporting. In some organizations, this centralized record is referred to as a “risk register.” OMB Circular A-11<sup>9</sup> describes a risk register as “a repository of risk information including the data understood about risks over time.” A-11 further explains, “Typically, a risk register contains a description of the risk, the impact if the risk should occur, the probability of its occurrence, mitigation strategies, risk owners, and a ranking to identify higher priority risks” [15].<sup>10</sup>
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティに関する所見、ギャップ、脆弱性を一元的な記録に集約することで、機関はサイバーセキュリティリスクの統合的な見方を得て、より十分な情報に基づくリスクの意思決定を行えます。たとえば、システムの認可の決定が機関全体にどのような影響を及ぼしうるか、またより広範なリスクの意思決定が複雑で相互接続されたインフラストラクチャでどのように展開しうるかを判断することが挙げられます。組織全体のリスクの記録により、一貫した報告が可能になります。組織によっては、この一元的な記録を「リスク登録簿」と呼びます。OMB Circular A-11<sup>9</sup> は、リスク登録簿を「リスクに関する情報（時間の経過とともに把握されたリスクに関するデータを含む）の保管場所」と説明しています。A-11 はさらに、「通常、リスク登録簿には、リスクの説明、リスクが発生した場合の影響、発生確率、軽減戦略、リスクの責任者、優先度の高いリスクを特定するための順位付けが含まれる」と説明しています [15]。<sup>10</sup>

contents.html: Using the Cybersecurity Framework, an organization can assemble system-level weaknesses or deficiencies into an enterprise-wide understanding of cybersecurity vulnerabilities. By discussing weaknesses or deficiencies that impact multiple systems or business units, the organization can develop consistent methods to identify, communicate, and plan mitigation activities. This information can be viewed at the Subcategory, Category, or Function level to provide agencies with additional context before making risk decisions and associated resource investments. While this integrated view may be helpful, agencies should exercise caution to prevent overextension of conclusions, especially if the impetus is to enable broad participation across the organization. The process of translating system risks into organizational risks should be thoroughly vetted by relevant cybersecurity experts to reduce distortions or oversimplifications before arriving at broader conclusions. Once the risk-rating mechanisms and processes are shown to be applied homogenously across systems, meaningful organization risks can be determined. Individual system risk ratings should first be shown to be objectively consistent and repeatable before broader implications can be considered reliable.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークを用いることで、組織は、システムレベルの弱点や欠陥を、エンタープライズ全体のサイバーセキュリティ脆弱性の理解へとまとめることができます。複数のシステムや事業部門に影響する弱点や欠陥について議論することで、組織は、軽減活動を特定し、伝え、計画するための一貫した方法を確立できます。この情報は、サブカテゴリ、カテゴリ、機能のいずれの水準でも確認でき、機関がリスクの意思決定と関連するリソースの投資を行う前に、追加の文脈を得られます。この統合的な見方は有用な場合がありますが、特に組織全体の幅広い参加を可能にすることが動機である場合には、機関は結論を過度に拡大解釈しないよう注意すべきです。システムのリスクを組織のリスクに置き換えるプロセスは、より広範な結論に至る前に、関連するサイバーセキュリティの専門家が徹底的に精査し、歪みや単純化しすぎを減らすべきです。リスク評価の仕組みとプロセスがシステム間で均質に適用されていることが示されて初めて、意味のある組織のリスクを判断できます。個々のシステムのリスク評価が客観的に一貫しており再現可能であることをまず示してから、より広範な含意を信頼できると考えるべきです。

contents.html: Further, aggregating essential information from SARs, POA&Ms, and SSPs enables security Authorization decisions through continuous monitoring. Security control assessments, remediation actions, and key updates to the SARs, POA&Ms, and SSPs for the system at hand can be considered in the context of the organization’s aggregate risk. The risk register is also curated using the ongoing risk changes tracked through RMF Monitor activities. A cybersecurity risk register is a tool that helps the AO understand if accepting the system risk will drive overall risk beyond the organization’s tolerance. Organizing a risk register using language from the Cybersecurity Framework Core enables a larger group of people to participate in and inform the authorization decision. In particular, the clear language of Functions and Categories of the Core enables broad participation.
contents.html_ja: さらに、SAR、POA&M、SSP から重要な情報を集約することで、継続的監視を通じたセキュリティの認可の決定が可能になります。当該システムの SAR、POA&M、SSP に対するセキュリティ管理策の評価、是正措置、主要な更新は、組織の集約されたリスクの文脈で検討できます。リスク登録簿は、RMF の Monitor 活動を通じて追跡される継続的なリスクの変化を用いて整備されます。サイバーセキュリティのリスク登録簿は、システムのリスクを受容することが、全体のリスクを組織の許容度を超えるものにしてしまうかどうかを AO が理解するのに役立つツールです。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのコアの言葉を用いてリスク登録簿を整理することで、より多くの人々が認可の決定に参加し、情報を提供できるようになります。特に、コアの機能とカテゴリの明確な言葉は、幅広い参加を可能にします。

contents.html: With a cybersecurity risk register informed by the Cybersecurity Framework Core, an organization can efficiently generate risk reports. Reports often need to be distributed to a variety of audiences, including business process personnel who manage risk as part of their daily responsibilities; senior executives who approve and are responsible for agency operations and investment strategies based on risk, other internal units; and external organizations. This means that reports need to be clear, understandable, and vary significantly in both transparency and detail, depending on the recipient and report requirement. Furthermore, reporting timelines need to match expectations of the receiving parties in order to minimize the time between the measurement of risk and delivery of the report. A standardized reporting format can assist agencies in meeting multiple cybersecurity reporting needs.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークのコアに基づくサイバーセキュリティのリスク登録簿があれば、組織はリスク報告書を効率的に作成できます。報告書は、さまざまな読み手に配布する必要があることが少なくありません。たとえば、日々の責務の一部としてリスクを管理する業務プロセスの担当者、リスクに基づく機関の運営や投資戦略を承認し責任を負う上級幹部、その他の内部部署、外部組織などです。このため、報告書は明確で分かりやすいものでなければならず、受け手や報告の要件に応じて、透明性と詳細さの両面で大きく異なる必要があります。さらに、リスクの測定から報告書の提供までの時間を最小限にするため、報告のタイムラインは受け手の期待に合致している必要があります。標準化された報告形式は、機関が複数のサイバーセキュリティ報告のニーズを満たす助けとなります。

contents.html: Today, risk reporting within federal organizations varies greatly and is performed using multiple technologies and reporting formats since different sources request information for different purposes. In part to address this variability, in recent years, the OMB has requested that annual FISMA metrics be organized using the structure of the Cybersecurity Framework’s Core. With an increasing number of federal organizations, partners, and suppliers using the Cybersecurity Framework, it is more efficient to use the Framework’s approach to meet these multiple reporting needs.
contents.html_ja: 現在、連邦組織内のリスク報告は大きく異なっており、情報の提供元ごとに目的が異なるため、複数の技術と報告形式を用いて行われています。このばらつきに対処する目的の一端として、近年、OMB は、毎年の FISMA 指標をサイバーセキュリティフレームワークのコアの構造に沿って整理するよう求めています。サイバーセキュリティフレームワークを用いる連邦組織、パートナー、供給者が増えているため、これら複数の報告ニーズを満たすには、フレームワークのアプローチを用いるほうが効率的です。

contents.html: Using standardized risk register categories such as the hierarchy of cybersecurity outcomes in the Core or the SP800-53 Control Families allows organizations to generate reports at varying levels of detail. Specifically, relating the hierarchy of five Functions, Categories, and Subcategories to SP 800-53 controls allows maximum flexibility in the level of detail of a given report and can make those reports more useful to varied audiences. That level of detail can be achieved quickly using the Core, thereby minimizing time and resources invested in generating the report.

contents.html: In the RMF, after the system is categorized as a high, moderate, or low impact (based on FIPS 199/SP 800-60), organizations leverage FIPS 200 to identify minimum security requirements associated with the system impact level [12][16][17]. They then use the SP 800-53 tailoring process to apply any other needed security to address specific mission objectives, operational constraints, cybersecurity requirements, and other organizational considerations. This process is used to customize the controls baseline for each system.
contents.html_ja: RMF では、システムが（FIPS 199／SP 800-60 に基づいて）High、Moderate、Low のいずれかの影響度にカテゴリ分類された後、組織は FIPS 200 を活用して、そのシステムの影響度に関連する最低限のセキュリティ要件を特定します [12][16][17]。その後、SP 800-53 のテーラリングプロセスを用いて、特定の任務目標、運用上の制約、サイバーセキュリティ要件、その他の組織上の考慮事項に対処するために必要なセキュリティ対策をさらに適用します。このプロセスは、システムごとに管理策ベースラインをカスタマイズするために用いられます。

contents.html: The Cybersecurity Framework offers a mechanism for reconciling mission objectives and cybersecurity requirements into Profiles, making them an important work product using a top-down approach to inform the tailoring. In developing a Profile, organizations can align and de-conflict all mission objectives and cybersecurity requirements into a singular structure according to the taxonomy of the Core. That allows organizations to easily prioritize the cybersecurity outcomes of the Subcategories and supports improved reporting. (Also see Use Case 7, above.) Since Profiles can be a reconciliation of cybersecurity requirements and associated priorities from many sources, they can be used as a concise and important tool when tailoring SP 800-53 initial control baselines to final control baselines. Specifically, considering organizational Subcategory priorities and knowing the associated SP 800-53 controls can help in precisely adjusting the controls baseline in ways that best support the organizational mission.
contents.html_ja: サイバーセキュリティフレームワークは、任務目標とサイバーセキュリティ要件を調整してプロファイルにまとめるしくみを提供します。これにより、プロファイルは、トップダウンのアプローチでテーラリングに情報を提供する重要な成果物となります。プロファイルを作成する際、組織は、すべての任務目標とサイバーセキュリティ要件を、コアの分類体系に従って単一の構造に整合させ、矛盾を解消できます。これにより、組織はサブカテゴリのサイバーセキュリティの成果に容易に優先順位を付けられ、報告の改善も支えられます（上記の利用例 7 も参照）。プロファイルは、多くの情報源からのサイバーセキュリティ要件と関連する優先事項を調整した結果となりうるため、SP 800-53 の初期の管理策ベースラインを最終的な管理策ベースラインへとテーラリングする際の、簡潔で重要なツールとして用いることができます。具体的には、組織のサブカテゴリの優先事項を考慮し、関連する SP 800-53 の管理策を把握することで、組織の任務を最もよく支える形で管理策ベースラインを精密に調整する助けとなります。

original_blocks.html: 1 Introduction

The increasing frequency, creativity, and variety of cybersecurity attacks means that all organizations should place great emphasis on managing cybersecurity risk as a part of their Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) programs to fulfill their mission and business objectives. By integrating the Cybersecurity Framework with NIST cybersecurity risk management standards and guidelines already in wide use at various organizational levels, agencies can develop, implement, and continuously improve agency-wide cybersecurity risk management processes that inform strategic, operational, and other enterprise risk decisions.1
1.1 Audience

This document is intended for those responsible for overseeing, leading, and managing information systems within their agencies. That includes senior executives, line managers, and staff. It is especially relevant for personnel who develop, implement, report, and improve enterprise and cybersecurity risk management processes within their organizations. While the focus is on federal users, NIST expects that many public and private sector organizations that

original_blocks.html: OMB Guidance Regarding Enterprise Risk Management The U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) evaluates, formulates, and coordinates management procedures and program objectives within and among federal departments and agencies. In that role, OMB provides guidance in the form of memoranda to federal managers regarding the management of risks (including information and technology risks) that may impact achievement of strategic objectives and that arise from agencies’ activities and operations. Circular A-130, Appendix III Responsibilities for Protecting Federal Information Resources, Section 4.n The [Cybersecurity] Framework is not intended to duplicate the current information security and risk management practices in place within the Federal Government. However, in the course of managing information security risk using the established NIST Risk Management Framework and associated security standards and guidelines required by FISMA, agencies can leverage the Cybersecurity Framework to complement their current information security programs. OMB Circular No. A-123, Management’s Responsibility for Enterprise Risk Management and Internal Control Purpose: This Circular defines management’s responsibilities for enterprise risk management (ERM) and internal control. The Circular provides updated implementation guidance to federal managers to improve accountability and effectiveness of federal programs as well as mission- support operations through implementation of ERM practices and by establishing, maintaining, and assessing internal control effectiveness. The Circular emphasizes the need to integrate and coordinate risk management and strong and effective internal control into existing business activities and as an integral part of managing an agency.

original_blocks.html: Federal agencies and contractors each have some cybersecurity and acquisition requirements in common, while others are organizationally specific.7 In the acquisition process, this often causes a misunderstanding of expectations between federal agencies and contractors and may limit government access to the best products and services – while increasing costs to offerors, agencies, and taxpayers. The Cybersecurity Framework can be used to translate risk management practices and to support federal agencies as they interact with suppliers, including service providers, product vendors, systems integrators, organizations within a regulated sector, and other private sector partners. For example, an agency could use the Cybersecurity Framework during its market research prior to soliciting for and selecting a vendor. Respondents can be encouraged to include their Cybersecurity Framework Profile in the reply to a request for information or a sources sought notice. A reply describing cybersecurity capabilities of a product or service that includes Cybersecurity Framework terminology would help the agency to better compare and contrast the cybersecurity capabilities of organizations, products, and services of respondents. Cybersecurity Framework Profile can be incorporated into the acquisition process as a foundation for evaluation criteria (agency), solicitation response (supplier), proposal/quote review (agency), minimum contract requirements (agency), contract compliance evidence (supplier), and contract compliance verification (agency). The use of Cybersecurity Framework Profiles allows suppliers the flexibility to select from among various standards and practices to meet federal agency-specific requirements while communicating their cybersecurity posture in a consistent way. It also provides agencies the means to consistently and objectively assess the cybersecurity posture of potential partners.

original_blocks.html: Implementation Tiers are not prescriptive, and there is no set requirement for an organization and all its sub-organizations to operate at Implementation Tier 4. Rather, Implementation Tiers can be used for informed trade-off analysis since there is a corresponding cost and risk tolerance associated with each Implementation Tier. For example, to balance finite resources across all agency cybersecurity considerations, it may be appropriate to operate at Implementation Tier 2 in one part of an agency so that the agency can afford to operate at Implementation Tier 4 elsewhere. One way that federal agencies may apply these trade-offs is via FIPS-199 categorizations [12]. An agency might view FIPS-199 High Impact and High Value Asset8 (HVA) systems as appropriate for higher Implementation Tiers. Conversely, the agency may determine that operating at a lower Implementation Tier for FIPS-199 Low Impact categorized systems is acceptable. Agencies can evaluate the Implementation Tier at which they are operating in comparison to the desired Tier. This process may identify gaps between the current and target Implementation Tier as well as steps that the organization can take to progress to a desired Tier. These gaps indicate that there is a difference between current and optimal cybersecurity risk management behaviors. Agency Implementation Tier targets may be influenced by external requirements, including OMB policies and OMB cross-agency priorities.

Benefit(s): • Assist agencies in critically evaluating their cybersecurity risk management behaviors and identifying opportunities for improvement. • Enable agencies to make informed trade-offs concerning the appropriateness of and investments in the cybersecurity of particular organizational units or systems.Primary SP 800-37 Level: 2 – Mission/Business Processes
Primary Cybersecurity Framework Component: Implementation Tiers
Summary: Implementation Tiers provide agencies with a basis for rationalizing different aspects of cybersecurity operations across an organization. The Information Technology Laboratory (ITL) at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) promotes the U.S. economy and public welfare by providing technical leadership for the Nation’s measurement and standards infrastructure. ITL develops tests, test methods, reference data, proof of concept implementations, and technical analyses to advance the development and productive use of information technology. ITL’s responsibilities include the development of management, administrative, technical, and physical standards and guidelines for the cost-effective security and privacy of other than national security-related information in federal information systems.

The document highlights examples for implementing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) in a manner that complements the use of other NIST security and privacy risk management standards, guidelines, and practices. These examples include support for an Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) approach in alignment with OMB and FISMA requirements that agency heads “manage risk commensurate with the magnitude of harm that would result from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of a federal information system or federal information.” The use of the Cybersecurity Framework’s components enable discussion about the various types of risk that might occur within federal organizations and promote conversations about how to determine the likelihood and potential consequences of risk events. These activities can then be combined with those described in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-37, Revision 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations; SP 800-39, Managing Information Security Risk; and other guidelines to form a comprehensive risk-based approach for security and privacy.

This risk-based approach will assist agencies in determining the risks that are relevant to its mission throughout the operational lifecycle and apply an appropriate type and degree of resources to treat those risks to an acceptable level. Examples in this publication will demonstrate the use of the Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF), and other models to evaluate and report agency goals and progress and to inform tailoring activities for managing cybersecurity risk appropriately. Use of a comprehensive cybersecurity risk-based approach, as demonstrated through these examples, supports agencies’ activities to meet their concurrent obligations to comply with the requirements of FISMA and Executive Order (EO) 13800.

All federal agencies are entrusted with safeguarding the information contained in their systems and ensuring that those systems operate securely and reliably. It is vital that agency personnel at all levels manage their assets wisely and address cybersecurity risks effectively. To do that, agencies need a holistic approach to their enterprises’ risk management that includes timely, streamlined approaches and automated tools.

As part of its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act as amended (FISMA), the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) develops standards and guidelines—including minimum requirements—to provide adequate information security for federal information and information systems [1]. This suite of security and privacy risk management standards and guidelines provides guidance for an integrated, organization-wide program to manage information security risk.

NIST produced this report to assist federal agencies in strengthening their cybersecurity risk management processes by highlighting example approaches for implementing the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) [5]. Developed by NIST in close collaboration with private and public sectors, the Cybersecurity Framework is a risk-based approach used voluntarily by organizations across the United States. Initially developed to address cybersecurity challenges in the Nation’s Critical Infrastructure (CI) sectors, the voluntary Framework is used by a variety of organizations across the world. The Cybersecurity Framework aligns with and complements NIST’s suite of security and privacy risk management standards and guidelines.

This report illustrates eight example approaches through which federal agencies can leverage the Cybersecurity Framework to address common cybersecurity-related responsibilities. By doing so, agencies can integrate the Cybersecurity Framework with key NIST cybersecurity risk management standards and guidelines that are already in wide use. These eight approaches support a mature agency-wide cybersecurity risk management program:

Report cybersecurity risks

As part of its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act as amended (FISMA), NIST develops standards and guidelines—including minimum requirements—to support information security for agency operations and assets. NIST guidelines fulfill the requirements of FISMA and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-130, and are used by agencies to develop, implement, and maintain cybersecurity and privacy programs [6]. They include Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS), Special Publications (SPs), and NIST Interagency Reports (NISTIRs).

The Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014 formally updated NIST’s role to include identifying and developing cybersecurity risk frameworks for voluntary use by critical infrastructure (CI) owners and operators. The frameworks’ subsequent widespread use and adoption demonstrates their universal applicability [7]. That statute’s assignments included work that NIST began in February 2013 as a result of Executive Order (EO) 13636, Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity [8], which directed the Department of Commerce to lead the development of a voluntary framework to reduce CI cybersecurity risks. Accordingly, NIST convened industry, academia, and government sectors to develop the Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (known as the Cybersecurity Framework) that consists of standards, methodologies, procedures, and processes that align policy, business, and technological approaches to address cybersecurity risks [5]. It offers a high-level vocabulary for cybersecurity risk management along with a set of cybersecurity outcomes and a methodology to assess and manage those outcomes.

NIST will work with federal agencies to assess the value of these eight approaches, identify additional examples, and understand how to better illustrate applications of the Cybersecurity Framework. Feedback will inform NIST as it incorporates Cybersecurity Framework concepts into cybersecurity risk management publications.
The approaches described in this publication demonstrate how agencies can leverage both the Cybersecurity Framework and the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) to:
Measure and improve cybersecurity performance at various organizational levels;
Organize communication about cybersecurity risk, activities, and results across the organization-wide risk management program; and
Align and prioritize cybersecurity requirements for use in the acquisition process and to inform the tailoring of controls.
Alignment between the Cybersecurity Framework and RMF is also detailed in the following two figures. The RMF describes three levels of organizational management as illustrated in Figure 1.

Figure 2 depicts federal cybersecurity risk management approaches (middle column) as aligned with these three levels. Most of the approaches addressed in this publication comport with the “Mission/Business Processes” (Level 2). One approach exemplifies use of the Cybersecurity Framework at the “Organization” level (Level 1), and another addresses the “System” level (Level 3). The order of the approaches is not intended to imply criticality or priority. Agencies can prioritize implementation to best support their own cybersecurity needs.

Since the Cybersecurity Framework uses risk management processes to inform and prioritize organizations’ cybersecurity decisions, it can be adapted to provide a flexible, risk-based implementation that can be used with a broad array of risk management processes. That includes not only SP 800-37 Rev. 2 cited above, but also SP 800-39, Managing Information Security Risk: Organization, Mission, and Information System View [3] which describes the risk management process and four distinct steps – Frame, Assess, Respond, and Monitor – used by federal organizations, and optionally employed by private sector organizations.

Organizations manage many types of risk. They develop policies to identify, assess, and mitigate adverse effects with cybersecurity dependencies across various types of enterprise risks. In addition to cybersecurity risks, other typical enterprise risks include safety, financial, program, acquisitions, supply chain, and privacy. Many of these other types of risk may also have cybersecurity risk implications or be impacted by cybersecurity. Some employ different terminologies and risk management approaches to make decisions. OMB Circular A-123 establishes an expectation for federal agencies to proactively consider and address risks through an integrated, organization-level view of events, conditions, or scenarios that impact mission achievement. Organizations may have established a unique lexicon for ERM that should be considered when communicating risks at the organization level. This necessitates coordination with existing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) functions on how to best incorporate and communicate cybersecurity risks at the organization and system levels.

The Cybersecurity Framework Core’s five “Functions”—Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover—offer a way to organize cybersecurity risk management activities at their highest levels that can be applied across risk management disciplines. These same five words are further classified into more specific meanings with the Cybersecurity Framework Core, enabling precise and efficient implementation of any enterprise risk decisions impacting cybersecurity. Many stakeholders from various parts of an organization can understand and may already use these five words in the context of risk decisions. Different disciplines communicate risk at differing levels of breadth and depth, so the Cybersecurity Framework outcomes help facilitate discussions.

When representatives across an enterprise are engaged in identifying and prioritizing organizational assets and determining risk management strategies supported by a common language, they are more likely to achieve the desired outcomes.
Summary of the Approach: Integrate Enterprise and Cybersecurity Risk Management

Federal agencies, like private sector organizations, are subject to multiple cybersecurity requirements. These include but are not limited to laws, regulations, oversight by and reports to Congress, internal policy, and OMB policies. Using Cybersecurity Framework Profiles, Federal agencies can manage requirements by integrating and prioritizing those requirements.

Agencies can align and merge internal and external requirements using the structure of the Core. For instance, a federal agency may need to abide by FISMA, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Security Rule, the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, and their own cybersecurity policy. Applicable excerpts of these laws, guidelines, policies, and objectives can be aligned with the various Functions, Categories, and Subcategories of the Core. That can help agencies to determine where requirements overlap and/or conflict so that they can consider alternative approaches—including modifying cybersecurity requirements within that agency’s control.

Stakeholder discussions regarding the Core outcomes help with prioritization. For instance, certain subcategory outcomes are meaningful for multiple requirements. It may also be clear that a short list of Subcategories is essential to achieve mission objectives. Where under investing in a given area might jeopardize those mission objectives, utilizing the structure of the Core as inputs can determine priorities and drive cybersecurity investments, effort, and focus.
Summary of the Approach: Manage Cybersecurity Requirements
Summary of the Approach: Integrate and Align Cybersecurity and Acquisition Processes

The Cybersecurity Framework’s Implementation Tiers are designed as an overarching measurement of cybersecurity risk management behaviors within an organization. They help an organization to consider the following cybersecurity properties on a scale from 1 to 4 (Partial, Risk-Informed, Repeatable, and Adaptive):
Risk Management Process – Does our organization have a cybersecurity risk management process that is functioning and repeatable?
Integrated Risk Management Program – To what extent is cybersecurity risk management integrated into enterprise risk management?
External Participation – To what degree is our organization (or units within the organization) sharing with and receiving cybersecurity information from outside parties?
Summary of the Approach: Evaluate Organizational Cybersecurity

The Core taxonomy of cybersecurity outcomes that are captured in Subcategories provides a logical structure to organize cybersecurity operations within an agency—specifically, how work is assigned, tracked, and measured and how personnel empowerment and accountability is managed.

The Cybersecurity Framework provides a way to assign cybersecurity responsibilities to units or individuals in an organization, including external entities with risk management roles. That allows executives to specify tasks, responsibilities, and risk management strategies. It also enables executives to empower units and individuals and to reward them appropriately. If parts of cybersecurity operations are not performing as intended, or if risk is above set threshold levels, the Cybersecurity Framework structure helps managers trace and investigate the situation and hold relevant units and individuals accountable.

Using a Cybersecurity Framework Profile also may help identify opportunities for improving management of the organization’s cybersecurity workforce and how it achieves defined risk tolerance outcomes. One way to do that is by applying the NICE Workforce Framework from the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE), documented in SP 800-181 [13]. That workforce framework serves as a fundamental reference. It offers organizations a consistent lexicon for categorizing and describing cybersecurity work by category, specialty area, and work role, as well as a superset of cybersecurity knowledge, skills, and abilities (KSAs) and tasks for each work role. These elements support consistent organizational and sector communication for cybersecurity education, training, and workforce development. While the Cybersecurity Framework and the NICE Framework were developed separately, they complement each other by describing a hierarchical approach to achieving cybersecurity goals. The NICE program is in the process of determining alignment among Cybersecurity Framework subcategory outcomes and NICE Work Roles. As this work progresses, the alignment will help agencies document current and desired outcomes (based on Framework Core Subcategories) as well as the types of personnel that might have a role in accomplishing those outcomes. Furthermore, with the knowledge of the potential NICE work roles associated with a given set of outcomes, agencies will also be able to consider the NICE Framework’s definition of tasks associated with those roles and the relevant knowledge, skills, and abilities. This may help agencies to better define personnel requirements, qualifications, and evaluation criteria.

In addition to determining the applicable work roles for a set of outcomes and associated security controls, the Cybersecurity Framework provides a manageable way to apportion responsibility for cybersecurity. Since the subcategory outcomes have already been mapped to the security controls in SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations, the responsibility for implementing and maintaining corresponding controls can also be assigned to these roles [14].

When analyzing the desired cybersecurity outcomes associated with the Core’s Categories and Subcategories, some outcomes may be managed centrally and more cost-effectively for the entire agency rather than separately by each organizational unit. For example, an agency may determine that it is most beneficial and cost-effective for the entire agency to make Subcategory PR.AC-2 (i.e., “physical access to assets is managed and protected”) the responsibility of the Physical Security unit. These determinations can assist federal agencies in identifying candidates for common and hybrid controls as specified in SP 800-53.

Another way for federal agencies to identify common cybersecurity controls is by identifying common assets and business processes. Managers of business units within agencies have key roles in identifying high-value assets and business processes. The ensuing discussions among business unit managers, the CISO, and other stakeholders regarding how to prioritize and protect these assets will likely recognize business units with similar assets or business processes that can utilize shared services. This can lead to the subsequent identification of common controls to secure assets and business processes across business units and potentially yield cost savings.
Summary of the Approach: Manage the Cybersecurity Program
By aggregating findings, agencies can:
Track planned security and privacy controls,
Assess the implementation of controls,
Annotate weaknesses or deficiencies in security controls,
Identify residual vulnerabilities in the system, and
Highlight mitigation plans.
The information in these key documents is used by Authorizing Officials (AO) to make risk-based authorization decisions.

Industry users of the Cybersecurity Framework have noted that differing elements of the organization may not consistently apply risk criteria. Many organizations have risk determination models like those described in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-30, Rev.1, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments [18]. Discussions among stakeholders about risk scales and risk criteria may help the organization to improve consistency and awareness, which may in turn support improved application of the RMF tasks and related activities.

Using the Cybersecurity Framework, an organization can assemble system-level weaknesses or deficiencies into an enterprise-wide understanding of cybersecurity vulnerabilities. By discussing weaknesses or deficiencies that impact multiple systems or business units, the organization can develop consistent methods to identify, communicate, and plan mitigation activities. This information can be viewed at the Subcategory, Category, or Function level to provide agencies with additional context before making risk decisions and associated resource investments. While this integrated view may be helpful, agencies should exercise caution to prevent overextension of conclusions, especially if the impetus is to enable broad participation across the organization. The process of translating system risks into organizational risks should be thoroughly vetted by relevant cybersecurity experts to reduce distortions or oversimplifications before arriving at broader conclusions. Once the risk-rating mechanisms and processes are shown to be applied homogenously across systems, meaningful organization risks can be determined. Individual system risk ratings should first be shown to be objectively consistent and repeatable before broader implications can be considered reliable.

Further, aggregating essential information from SARs, POA&Ms, and SSPs enables security Authorization decisions through continuous monitoring. Security control assessments, remediation actions, and key updates to the SARs, POA&Ms, and SSPs for the system at hand can be considered in the context of the organization’s aggregate risk. The risk register is also curated using the ongoing risk changes tracked through RMF Monitor activities. A cybersecurity risk register is a tool that helps the AO understand if accepting the system risk will drive overall risk beyond the organization’s tolerance. Organizing a risk register using language from the Cybersecurity Framework Core enables a larger group of people to participate in and inform the authorization decision. In particular, the clear language of Functions and Categories of the Core enables broad participation.
Summary of Approach: Maintain a Comprehensive Understanding of Cybersecurity Risk

With a cybersecurity risk register informed by the Cybersecurity Framework Core, an organization can efficiently generate risk reports. Reports often need to be distributed to a variety of audiences, including business process personnel who manage risk as part of their daily responsibilities; senior executives who approve and are responsible for agency operations and investment strategies based on risk, other internal units; and external organizations. This means that reports need to be clear, understandable, and vary significantly in both transparency and detail, depending on the recipient and report requirement. Furthermore, reporting timelines need to match expectations of the receiving parties in order to minimize the time between the measurement of risk and delivery of the report. A standardized reporting format can assist agencies in meeting multiple cybersecurity reporting needs.

Today, risk reporting within federal organizations varies greatly and is performed using multiple technologies and reporting formats since different sources request information for different purposes. In part to address this variability, in recent years, the OMB has requested that annual FISMA metrics be organized using the structure of the Cybersecurity Framework’s Core. With an increasing number of federal organizations, partners, and suppliers using the Cybersecurity Framework, it is more efficient to use the Framework’s approach to meet these multiple reporting needs.

Using standardized risk register categories such as the hierarchy of cybersecurity outcomes in the Core or the SP800-53 Control Families allows organizations to generate reports at varying levels of detail. Specifically, relating the hierarchy of five Functions, Categories, and Subcategories to SP 800-53 controls allows maximum flexibility in the level of detail of a given report and can make those reports more useful to varied audiences. That level of detail can be achieved quickly using the Core, thereby minimizing time and resources invested in generating the report.
Summary of Approach: Report Cybersecurity Risks
Information systems are most valuable when their features explicitly support an organization’s mission objectives and requirements.

In the RMF, after the system is categorized as a high, moderate, or low impact (based on FIPS 199/SP 800-60), organizations leverage FIPS 200 to identify minimum security requirements associated with the system impact level [12][16][17]. They then use the SP 800-53 tailoring process to apply any other needed security to address specific mission objectives, operational constraints, cybersecurity requirements, and other organizational considerations. This process is used to customize the controls baseline for each system.

The Cybersecurity Framework offers a mechanism for reconciling mission objectives and cybersecurity requirements into Profiles, making them an important work product using a top-down approach to inform the tailoring. In developing a Profile, organizations can align and de-conflict all mission objectives and cybersecurity requirements into a singular structure according to the taxonomy of the Core. That allows organizations to easily prioritize the cybersecurity outcomes of the Subcategories and supports improved reporting. (Also see Use Case 7, above.) Since Profiles can be a reconciliation of cybersecurity requirements and associated priorities from many sources, they can be used as a concise and important tool when tailoring SP 800-53 initial control baselines to final control baselines. Specifically, considering organizational Subcategory priorities and knowing the associated SP 800-53 controls can help in precisely adjusting the controls baseline in ways that best support the organizational mission.
Summary of Approach: Inform the Tailoring Process
